source: The lipid density is present, however, at this location for the simulated open Ca2+-bound WT TMEM16F (6QP6*, initiated from PDB ID 6QP6) and closed Ca2+-bound WT TMEM16F (PDB ID 6QP6) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The loss of density indicates that the normal membrane contact with the protein near the TMEM16F groove has been compromised in the mutant structure.
source: The loss of density indicates that the normal membrane contact with the protein near the TMEM16F groove has been compromised in the mutant structure.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the observed loss of lipid density in simulations.

claim: Residues in the site near the extracellular groove entrance on nhTMEM16 and TMEM16F seem to play a role in scrambling, but the mechanism by which they do so is unclear.
source: Residues in this site on nhTMEM16 and TMEM16F also seem to play a role in scrambling, but the mechanism by which they do so is unclear (Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a; Feng et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: Headgroup density isosurfaces from CGMD simulations of known scramblases bound to Ca2+ and with clear separation of TM4 and TM6 show that lipid headgroups occupy the full length of the groove creating a clear pathway that links the upper and lower membrane leaflets.
source: Headgroup density isosurfaces from CGMD simulations of known scramblases bound to Ca2+ and with clear separation of TM4 and TM6 show that lipid headgroups occupy the full length of the groove creating a clear pathway that links the upper and lower membrane leaflets (nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) and TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J), Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Simulation-derived densities crossing the bilayer are strikingly similar to lipids resolved in cryo-EM structures of fungal scramblases in nanodisc.
source: These simulation-derived densities crossing the bilayer are strikingly similar to lipids resolved in cryo-EM structures of fungal scramblases in nanodisc (Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental cryo-EM data.

claim: Open-groove structures typically have an average of 2–3 lipids in the TM4/TM6 groove at any given time.
source: Open-groove structures typically have an average of 2–3 lipids in the TM4/TM6 groove at any given time (see Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: All of the grooves are filled with water.
source: Additional analysis shows that all of the grooves are filled with water (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Apo and closed Ca2+-bound TMEM16 structures lack lipid headgroup density spanning the bilayer.
source: Unlike the open Ca2+-bound scramblase structures, apo and closed Ca2+-bound TMEM16 structures lack lipid headgroup density spanning the bilayer, and their density profiles are more consistent across the entire family (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Simulation of a Ca2+-bound TMEM16A conformation that conducts Cl− in AAMD samples partial lipid headgroup penetration into the extracellular vestibule but lipids fail to traverse the bilayer.
source: Similarly, simulation of a Ca2+-bound TMEM16A conformation that conducts Cl− in AAMD (7ZK3*6, initiated from PDB ID 7ZK3, see Appendix 1—Methods and Appendix 1—figure 1) samples partial lipid headgroup penetration into the extracellular vestibule formed by TM3/TM6, but lipids fail to traverse the bilayer as indicated by the lack of density in the center of the membrane (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The lack of lipid traversal in TMEM16A simulations is consistent with TMEM16A lacking scramblase activity.
source: This finding is consistent with TMEM16A lacking scramblase activity (Han et al., 2019; Gyobu et al., 2017); however, we simulated another ion-conductive TMEM16A conformation that can achieve a fully lipid-lined groove during its simulation (Figure 1D), although this configuration was uncommon (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from cited studies.

claim: The strongest scrambler was the open-groove, Ca2+-bound fungal nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), with 24.4 ± 5.2 events per μs.
source: The strongest scrambler was the open-groove, Ca2+-bound fungal nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), with 24.4 ± 5.2 events per μs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The open Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 6QM6) scrambled lipids at 15.7 ± 3.9 events per μs, in line with experimental findings.
source: In line with experimental findings, the open Ca2+-free structure (PDB ID 6QM6), which is structurally very similar to PDB ID 4WIS, also scrambled lipids (15.7 ± 3.9 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Kalienkova et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data, comparison with experimental findings, and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: No scrambling events were observed for the intermediate- (PDB ID 6QMA) and closed- (PDB ID 6QM4, PDB ID 6QMB) groove nhTMEM16 structures.
source: In contrast, we observed no scrambling events for the intermediate- (PDB ID 6QMA) and closed- (PDB ID 6QM4, PDB ID 6QMB) groove nhTMEM16 structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: The open Ca2+-bound cryo-EM structure of afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG) is scrambling competent at 10.7 ± 2.9 events per μs.
source: We observed a similar trend for the fungal afTMEM16, where our simulations identified the open Ca2+-bound cryo-EM structure (PDB ID 7RXG) as scrambling competent (10.7 ± 2.9 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) while the Ca2+-free closed-groove structure (PDB ID 7RXB) was not.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The Ca2+-free closed-groove afTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 7RXB) is not scrambling competent.
source: We observed a similar trend for the fungal afTMEM16, where our simulations identified the open Ca2+-bound cryo-EM structure (PDB ID 7RXG) as scrambling competent (10.7 ± 2.9 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) while the Ca2+-free closed-groove structure (PDB ID 7RXB) was not.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: The Ca2+-bound X-ray structure of TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) facilitates scrambling at 8.2 ± 2.9 events per μs in line with experiments in the presence of Ca2+.
source: For TMEM16K, our simulations showed that the Ca2+-bound X-ray structure (PDB ID 5OC9) facilitates scrambling (8.2 ± 2.9 events per μs) in line with experiments in the presence of Ca2+, when the groove is presumably open, and previous MD simulations (Bushell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data, comparison with experimental findings, and citation to previous simulations.

claim: There is a stark asymmetry in the number of scrambling events between the two monomers of TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9), with >80% of events happening via chain B.
source: Interestingly, we found a stark asymmetry in the number of scrambling events between the two monomers, with >80% of events happening via chain B (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Chain B of TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) has a slightly wider ER lumen-facing entrance to the groove in the experimental starting structure and spontaneously opened its groove more than subunit A during the simulation.
source: Although both monomers are Ca2+-bound, chain B has a slightly wider endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen-facing entrance to the groove in the experimental starting structure (PDB ID 5OC9, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) and spontaneously opened its groove more than subunit A during the simulation (8.2 ± 1.3 Å compared to 5.8 ± 0.6 Å on average, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A), which likely accounts for the increased rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and structural comparison, and is illustrated in figures.

claim: The closed-groove TMEM16K conformation (PDB ID 6R7X) showed very little scrambling activity (0.4 ± 0.7 events per μs).
source: The closed-groove TMEM16K conformation (PDB ID 6R7X) showed very little scrambling activity (0.4 ± 0.7 events per μs).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: None of the WT TMEM16F structures solved to date have exhibited an open hydrophilic groove, even those determined under activating conditions.
source: Although TMEM16F is a known lipid scramblase found in the plasma membrane of platelets (Suzuki et al., 2010), none of the WT structures solved to date, even those determined under activating conditions, have exhibited an open hydrophilic groove.
evidence: This claim is based on review of structural data and is supported by a citation.

claim: Simulations of 10 WT TMEM16F structures observed little to no lipid scrambling in each case.
source: We simulated 10 of these proteins and observed little to no lipid scrambling in each case (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Mutations at position F518 turn TMEM16F into a constitutively active scramblase.
source: Others have shown that mutations at position F518 turn TMEM16F into a constitutively active scramblase (Le et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The F518H mutant (PDB ID 8B8J) is structurally characterized by a kink in TM3, and TM4 pulls away from TM6 35° compared to a closed WT TMEM16F structure (PDB ID 6QP6).
source: The F518H mutant (PDB ID 8B8J) is structurally characterized by a kink in TM3, and TM4 pulls away from TM6 35° compared to a closed WT TMEM16F structure (PDB ID 6QP6) (Arndt et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J) was the only system initiated directly from a solved structure that showed scrambling activity at 11.3 ± 1.6 events per μs.
source: In our simulations, TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J) was the only system initiated directly from a solved structure that showed scrambling activity (11.3 ± 1.6 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: A WT TMEM16F with a single open groove obtained from AAMD (6QP6*) showed moderate lipid scrambling activity at 3.0 ± 1.6 events per μs, most of which happened through the open groove.
source: Additionally, we performed CGMD on a WT TMEM16F with a single open groove obtained from AAMD initiated from a closed-state structure (cluster 10 in Khelashvili et al., 2022, 6QP6* in Figure 2A). We observed moderate lipid scrambling activity (3.0 ± 1.6 events per μs), most of which happened through the open groove (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: The rates of scrambling are higher for the TMEM16F F518H mutant than the open WT TMEM16F, but there were no noticeable differences in how lipids enter the pathway or how long they take to transition.
source: Although the rates of scrambling are higher for the mutant than the open WT TMEM16F, there were no noticeable differences in how lipids enter the pathway or how long they take to transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental structures of TMEM16A failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations.
source: Finally, we simulated six structures of mouse TMEM16A, which functions as an ion channel but lacks lipid scrambling activity (Paulino et al., 2017). As expected, both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental structures failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations, as did one alternative and two ion conduction-competent structures that were obtained from AAMD (see Appendix 1—Methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and comparison with experimental findings.

claim: A TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*) scrambled a single lipid through each groove in a manner nearly identical to the scramblases.
source: However, a TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*, simulations initiated from PDB ID 5OYB; Jia and Chen, 2021) did scramble a single lipid through each groove in a manner nearly identical to the scramblases (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A, E and Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model.
source: In our CGMD simulations, 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model, which we refer to as 'in-the-groove' scrambling (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is presented in a table.

claim: All TMEM16 structures thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity.
source: Interestingly, all the TMEM16 structures included in this study thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: Negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) was observed in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å.
source: We observed negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and at the same time do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å (Figure 3A, upper left quadrant).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: All active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å.
source: On the other hand, all active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: The highest scrambling rates were observed in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation.
source: Among these structures, we observed the highest scrambling rates in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation (shaded region).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: Two TMEM16F structures (PDB ID 8B8J and 6QP6*) spent less than half of their simulation time in an open configuration and had scrambling rates similar to or less than half of rates for the open scramblases.
source: To the left of this shaded area, there are two TMEM16F structures (PDB ID 8B8J and 6QP6*) that spent less than half of their simulation time in an open configuration (note large error bars and Figure 3B) and had scrambling rates similar to (PDB ID 8B8J) or less than half of (6QP6*) rates for the open scramblases (PDB IDs 6QM6, 7RXG, and 5OC9).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves.
source: Although these results indicate that scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves, we want to clarify that lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness.
source: Although these results indicate that scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves, we want to clarify that lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The extremely thin membranes are likely correlated with groove opening, rather than being an independent contributing factor to lipid scrambling.
source: Therefore, we argue that the extremely thin membranes are likely correlated with groove opening, rather than being an independent contributing factor to lipid scrambling.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the simulation data and represents the authors' argument.

claim: The major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove.
source: Thus, the major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of simulation data.

claim: Hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the TMEM16F pathway dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through.
source: Upon closer inspection of TMEM16F, we noticed that hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the pathway, previously identified as an activation gate (Le et al., 2019b), dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C; Figure 3—videos 3 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures and videos.

claim: The distribution of the groove distances is similar for both TMEM16F structures that exhibit scrambling (8B8J and 6QP6*), but the WT open structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate.
source: Although the distribution of the groove distances is similar for both TMEM16F structures that exhibit scrambling (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B), the WT open structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Similar fluctuations were observed in both subunits of the open asymmetric TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) which transiently constrict the lipid pathway at Y366/I370/T435/L436.
source: We observed similar fluctuations in both subunits of the open asymmetric TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) which transiently constrict the lipid pathway at Y366/I370/T435/L436 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A, D; Figure 3—videos 2 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures and videos.

claim: The TMEM16K subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration.
source: Again, we observed that the subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F.
source: Qualitatively, scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F (black dots in Figure 3B), while the consistently open Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 4WIS) allows lipid headgroups to scramble in an uninterrupted fashion (Figure 3B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qualitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure and video.

claim: The predicted ion-conductive state of TMEM16A (5OYB*) samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close, but just below, the empirically determined 6 Å threshold for scrambling.
source: Although all structures of TMEM16A, which is not a scramblase, have negligible scrambling in the groove, we did observe two events for a predicted ion-conductive state (5OYB*) which samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close, but just below, to the empirically determined 6 Å threshold for scrambling (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipid headgroups are observed throughout the TMEM16A pathway, but the flow of lipid is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass.
source: We observed lipid headgroups throughout the pathway, but just as for the TMEM16F and K structures, the flow of lipid is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and in TMEM16A they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipids in the TMEM16A pore are notably more stagnant than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645.
source: Lipids are also notably more stagnant in the pore than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645 (Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a video.

claim: Scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the TMEM16 family.
source: Despite these individual differences in groove dynamics, scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the family.
evidence: This claim is a generalization based on analysis of simulation data across multiple family members.

claim: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns.
source: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: Longer dwell times were observed for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove.
source: However, we observed longer dwell times for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT).
source: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT) (Appendix 1—figure 3A) with similar kinetics among the homologs and a mean diffusion coefficient between 10 and 16 Å2/ns (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Scrambling events enter and leave the groove at random locations with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8.
source: Scrambling events also enter and leave the groove at random locations (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5) with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8 (Figure 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: Four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove were previously hypothesized to help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids.
source: We previously identified four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove that we hypothesized help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids (Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim references a previous hypothesis from a cited study and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: CGMD of nhTMEM16 shows that although the four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble.
source: However, our CGMD of the same nhTMEM16 structure shows that although these residues have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases.
source: Lastly, the in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases (Appendix 1—figure 5), indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
source: Lastly, the in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases (Appendix 1—figure 5), indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Poisson distribution of scrambling events.

claim: Permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average.
source: As expected, permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average, while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 permeation events per μs on average.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of water permeation from simulation data.

claim: Dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 water permeation events per μs on average.
source: As expected, permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average, while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 permeation events per μs on average.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of water permeation from simulation data.

claim: Even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
source: Nonetheless, even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane (Appendix 1—figure 2A, closed).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: In open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets.
source: We qualitatively observed that in open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets (Appendix 1—figure 2A, open) as seen in fully atomistic simulations (Bushell et al., 2019; Stansfeld et al., 2015; Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Jiang et al., 2017; Khelashvili et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2022; Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021; Le et al., 2019b; Khelashvili et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data, comparison with atomistic simulations, and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore was observed, in line with the known ion-conducting capacity of these proteins.
source: We also observed spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore (Appendix 1—figure 2B; number of permeation events in Source data 1), in line with the known ion-conducting capacity of these proteins (Yang et al., 2012; Martins et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2010; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Bushell et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Scudieri et al., 2015; Falzone et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2022; Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data, comparison with experimental findings, and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Of the fungal structures, only the scrambling-competent open states sampled multiple ion permeation events with Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showing highest conductance.
source: Of the fungal structures, only the scrambling-competent open states sampled multiple ion permeation events with Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showing highest conductance followed by Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), which was 3 times lower, and then Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), which was another three times lower again.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claim: Cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 were measured for Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), and Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), respectively.
source: We also measured cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 for each simulation, respectively, computed from the ratio of total counts (PNa/PCl).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claim: The simulations are consistent with experiments showing that both fungal scramblases transport anions and cations, and both are weakly cation selective.
source: Our simulations are consistent with experiments showing that both fungal scramblases transport anions and cations (Lee et al., 2016), and both are weakly cation selective (PK/PCl = 1.5 for afTMEM16 based on experiment [Malvezzi et al., 2013] and PNa/PCl = 8.7 for nhTMEM16 based on AAMD [Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021]).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental and computational data from cited studies.

claim: CGMD simulations sample ion conduction through open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J, PNa/PCl = 1.3), which had the most ion permeation events.
source: Our CGMD simulations also sample ion conduction through open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J, PNa/PCl = 1.3), which had the most ion permeation events (Hunter, 2007) across the family, simulated open TMEM16F (6QP6*, PNa/PCl = 0.33), and open TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9, PNa/PCl = 1.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claim: The TMEM16K simulation result qualitatively agrees with experiment showing a slight cation preference.
source: This latter result on TMEM16K qualitatively agrees with experiment showing a slight cation preference (Bushell et al., 2019), while experimental results for TMEM16F are more complex as its ion selectivity depends on membrane potential and divalent/monovalent cation concentrations (Nguyen et al., 2021; Stabilini et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from cited studies.

claim: The simulation of the TMEM16F F518H mutant in 150 mM NaCl is most close to whole cell recordings performed in intracellular 150 mM NaCl and 15 μM Ca2+ where PNa/PCl = 1.0 ± 0.1, which is very similar to the simulated value of 1.3.

evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with other computational data from a cited study.

source: Surprisingly, most of these events happened at the dimer interface with lipids inserting their headgroups into the cavity outlined by TM3 and TM10 (Figure 4A, B; Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5).

claim: Out-of-the-groove scrambling at the dimer interface was only observed in simulations of the mammalian homologs.

evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claim: The dimer interface is largely hydrophobic, but there are a few polar and charged residues in the cavity near the membrane core, and water is present in the lower half of the cavity.
source: Although the dimer interface is largely hydrophobic, there are a few polar and charged residues in the cavity near the membrane core, and water is present in the lower half of the cavity (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).

claim: The headgroup of the lipid in the atomistic simulation of TMEM16F interacts with a glutamate (E843) and lysine (K850) on TM10 near the membrane midplane.
source: In fact, the headgroup of the lipid in our atomistic simulation of TMEM16F interacts with a glutamate (E843) and lysine (K850) on TM10 near the membrane midplane (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from atomistic simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipids that scramble at the dimer interface interact with the protein up to 10-fold longer on average than those in the canonical groove.
source: Lipids that scramble at the dimer interface interact with the protein up to 10-fold longer on average than those in the canonical groove (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: The most prolonged interactions occur at sites containing aromatic residues into which the lipid tails intercalate.
source: The most prolonged interactions occur at sites containing aromatic residues into which the lipid tails intercalate (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: One scrambling event occurred across a closed TM4/TM6 groove of Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6P47), which is the only event that fits the postulated out-of-the-groove definition where scrambling is expected to take place near TM4/TM6 but without inserting into the groove.
source: There were five more out-of-the-groove events, including one that occurred across a closed TM4/TM6 groove of Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6P47). From all our observed scrambling events, this is the only one that fits the postulated out-of-the-groove definition where scrambling is expected to take place near TM4/TM6 but without inserting into the groove (Feng et al., 2024b; Appendix 1—figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Two scrambling events occurred concurrently along TM6 and TM8 near the hydrophilic groove of a Ca2+-bound closed TMEM16F (PDB ID 8TAG).
source: Two events occurred concurrently along TM6 and TM8 again near the hydrophilic groove of a Ca2+-bound closed TMEM16F (PDB ID 8TAG; Appendix 1—figure 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Two scrambling events occurred along TM3 and TM4, one near the canonical TM4/TM6 groove of an open nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) and the other adjacent to the pore of an ion-conductive TMEM16A (7ZK3*8).
source: Lastly, two events occurred along TM3 and TM4, one near the canonical TM4/TM6 groove of an open nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) and the other adjacent to the pore of an ion-conductive TMEM16A (7ZK3*8; Appendix 1—figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: In each of the five out-of-the-groove events, the scrambling lipid traverses with two to four water molecules around its headgroup.
source: In each of these five out-of-the-groove events, the scrambling lipid traverses with two to four water molecules around its headgroup.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claim: Previous all-atom simulations of TMEM16 have captured partial translocations or at most a handful of complete scrambling events due to the challenges inherent in simulating molecular events on the low microseconds time scale.
source: Previous all-atom simulations of TMEM16 have captured partial translocations or – at most – a handful of complete scrambling events (e.g., Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Lee et al., 2018; Khelashvili et al., 2022) due to the challenges inherent in simulating molecular events on the low microseconds time scale.
evidence: This claim is based on review of previous computational studies and identifies a limitation.

claim: The small number of AAMD-derived scrambling events cannot provide rigorous statistics on scrambling rates, nor can they be leveraged to perform a large high-throughput comparison between the various family members.
source: Although this small number of AAMD-derived scrambling events yielded key insights into specific protein–lipid interactions and scrambling pathways, they cannot provide rigorous statistics on scrambling rates, nor can they be leveraged to perform a large high-throughput comparison between the various family members.
evidence: This claim is an assessment of the limitations of previous AAMD studies.

claim: The study used CGMD to systematically quantify lipid scrambling by five TMEM16 family members and relate their scrambling competence to their structural characteristics and ability to distort the membrane.
source: To circumvent sampling issues, we used CGMD to systematically quantify lipid scrambling by five TMEM16 family members and relate their scrambling competence to their structural characteristics and ability to distort the membrane.
evidence: This claim describes the approach and goals of the study.

claim: The simulations correctly differentiate between open and closed conformations across the five family members, consistent with a recent study showing good qualitative agreement between in vitro and in silico lipid scrambling using the same Martini 3 force field.
source: Our simulations correctly differentiate between open and closed conformations across the five family members, consistent with a recent study that showed good qualitative agreement between in vitro and in silico lipid scrambling using the same Martini 3 force field on a diverse set of proteins, including some TMEM16s (Tsuji et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data and a cited validation study.

claim: The simulation results are in accord with the general finding that TMEM16s show very little to no ion selectivity, although permeability ratios vary depending on ion concentrations and lipid environments.
source: In addition to lipid scrambling ability, our results are in accord with the general finding that TMEM16s show very little to no ion selectivity, although permeability ratios vary depending on ion concentrations and lipid environments (Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021; Nguyen et al., 2021; Stabilini et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental findings from cited studies.

claim: The study is in a unique position to directly compare a host of biophysical properties between different TMEM16 family members and their structures because the simulation conditions and system setups were identical in all simulations.
source: Because the simulation conditions and system setups were identical in all our simulations, we are in a unique position to directly compare a host of biophysical properties between different TMEM16 family members and their structures to answer ongoing questions in the field.
evidence: This claim highlights a methodological strength of the study.

claim: Even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit large membrane distortions.
source: We (Bethel and Grabe, 2016) and others Bushell et al., 2019; Khelashvili et al., 2019; Falzone et al., 2022; Arndt et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2019 have hypothesized that thinning lowers the physical and energetic barrier for lipid scrambling, but what is surprising is that even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit such large membrane distortions.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and comparison with previous hypotheses.

claim: Several of the closed-groove TMEM16F structures and the ion channel TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) compress the membrane 13–14 Å, yet these conformations do not induce scrambling.
source: For instance, several of the closed-groove TMEM16F structures and the ion channel TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) compress the membrane 13–14 Å. Despite this large deformation, these conformations do not induce scrambling.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: Structures with dilated grooves exhibit robust scrambling and thin the membrane another 3–4 Å, resulting in the most distorted bilayers.
source: On the other hand, structures with dilated grooves exhibit robust scrambling and thin the membrane another 3–4 Å, resulting in the most distorted bilayers.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: Because extreme membrane thinning is coupled to lipid entry into the upper and lower vestibules upon groove opening, it is difficult to determine how much the membrane thinning alone contributes to the resulting scramblase activity.
source: However, because this extreme membrane thinning is coupled to lipid entry into the upper and lower vestibules upon groove opening, it is difficult to determine how much the membrane thinning alone contributes to the resulting scramblase activity.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the simulation data.

claim: Groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling.
source: Thus, we conclude that groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling, and the importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of simulation data.

claim: The importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
source: Thus, we conclude that groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling, and the importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
evidence: This claim acknowledges an open question that remains to be addressed.

claim: The open-groove nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) is the fastest scrambler, with a rate twice as high as the other homologs.
source: Of the scrambling-competent TMEM16 structures, the open-groove nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) is the fastest scrambler, with a rate twice as high as the other homologs (Figures 2A and 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claim: On average, the groove width and membrane thinning of nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) are similar (within 1–2 Å) to the other robust scramblers nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), and TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9).
source: Yet on average, its groove width and membrane thinning are similar (within 1–2 Å) to the other robust scramblers nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), and TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: There are other features that impact scrambling rates, for example, the shape of the membrane distortion, groove dynamics, and residues lining the groove.
source: This suggests that there are other features that impact the rates, for example, the shape of the membrane distortion, groove dynamics, and residues lining the groove.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation data.

claim: Mixed membranes and membranes of shorter or longer chain length would be expected to alter lipid scrambling rates.
source: Another feature we have not explored is mixed membranes and membranes of shorter or longer chain length, which we expect would alter lipid scrambling rates.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about factors not explored in the study.

claim: TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane.
source: For example, TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane (Bushell et al., 2019; Petkovic et al., 2019; Bruininks et al., 2019), and TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes (Bushell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and computational studies.

claim: TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes.
source: For example, TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane (Bushell et al., 2019; Petkovic et al., 2019; Bruininks et al., 2019), and TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes (Bushell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a computational study.

claim: Experimental scrambling assays performed by different groups have reported basal level scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ for fungal and mammalian dual-function scramblases.
source: Experimental scrambling assays performed by different groups have reported basal level scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ for fungal and mammalian dual-function scramblases (Malvezzi et al., 2013; Bushell et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Brunner et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018; Malvezzi et al., 2018; Watanabe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: It is unknown where closed-groove scrambling takes place on the protein.
source: It is unknown where closed-groove scrambling takes place on the protein (Feng et al., 2024a) and simulations have never reported such events despite Li and co-workers reporting scrambling events for simulations initiated from closed TMEM16A, TMEM16K, and TMEM16F (Tsuji et al., 2019), which may have also been sampled in these trajectories.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge and references a citation.

claim: In aggregate, 60 scrambling events were observed that do not follow the credit card model and occur 'out-of-the-groove'.
source: In aggregate, we observed 60 scrambling events that do not follow the credit card model and occur 'out-of-the-groove' (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is presented in a table.

claim: Nearly all out-of-the-groove events (56/60) happen at the dimer interface between TM3 and TM10 of the opposite subunit.
source: Nearly all these events (56/60) happen at the dimer interface between TM3 and TM10 of the opposite subunit, hereon referred to as the dimer cleft.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: No scrambling at the dimer cleft was observed for any of the fungal structures.
source: Curiously, we do not observe scrambling at this location for any of the fungal structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claim: Mammalian TMEM16s have a ~4–5 Å wider gap on average at the lower leaflet dimer cleft entrance than the open fungal TMEM16s.
source: Although mammalian TMEM16s have a ~4–5 Å wider gap on average at the lower leaflet dimer cleft entrance than the open fungal TMEM16s, we do not always observe scrambling at such distances and sometimes do not observe any scrambling when the cleft is at its widest (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Lipids from both leaflets intercalate between TM3 and TM10 for all structures, which is consistent with lipid densities in cryo-EM nanodiscs images of fungal TMEM16s and TMEM16F.
source: For all structures, we see lipids from both leaflets intercalate between TM3 and TM10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), which is consistent with lipid densities in cryo-EM nanodiscs images of fungal TMEM16s (Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a) and TMEM16F (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and comparison with experimental cryo-EM data.

claim: The dimer interface may be a source for Ca2+-independent scrambling.
source: Based on our simulations, this interface may be a source for Ca2+-independent scrambling.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation data, indicated by 'may be'.

claim: It is unclear whether the out-of-the-groove events observed reflect the same closed-groove scrambling activity seen in experimental assays.
source: It is unclear whether the out-of-the-groove events we have observed reflect the same closed-groove scrambling activity seen in experimental assays (Lee et al., 2018; Malvezzi et al., 2018; Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a).
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty in interpreting the simulation results and references experimental studies.

claim: It is possible that slow or rare out-of-the-groove events were missed due to limited sampling.
source: Also, it is possible that we have missed slow or rare out-of-the-groove events due to limited sampling.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a potential limitation of the simulation study.

claim: Feng et al. reported a 7- to 18-fold increase in scrambling rate by nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions.
source: Feng et al. reported a 7- to 18-fold increase in scrambling rate by nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions (Feng et al., 2024a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Based on the open-groove count of 220 for nhTMEM16, 12–30 events would be expected for the closed-groove states, but no events were observed.
source: Based on our open-groove count of 220, we would expect 12–30 events for the closed-groove states, but we observed no events.
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from simulation data and comparison with experimental ratios.

claim: Watanabe et al. reported a six- to seven-fold increase in scrambling rate by TMEM16F in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions.
source: However, Watanabe et al. reported a six- to seven-fold increase in scrambling rate by TMEM16F in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions (Watanabe et al., 2018), which is consistent with the seven- to nine-fold increase revealed in our simulations between closed Ca2+-free TMEM16F structures (PBD IDs 6P47 and 6QPB) and the WT open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (6QP6*).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claim: Out-of-the-groove scrambling may be highly dependent on the membrane composition, and the scrambling ratios observed in DOPC may be different from the experimental rates determined in different lipids.
source: It is possible that out-of-the-groove scrambling is highly dependent on the membrane composition, as discussed earlier, and the scrambling ratios we observe in DOPC may be different from the experimental rates determined in different lipids.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about factors that may affect the results.

claim: The simulations observe much higher scrambling rates through the open grooves and much smaller flipping rates elsewhere on the protein or with closed-groove structures, suggesting that the simulations may be revealing aspects of Ca2+-independent scrambling in mammalian family members.
source: That said, we are encouraged by the high-level correspondence in TMEM16F – we observe much higher scrambling rates through the open grooves and much smaller flipping rates elsewhere on the protein or with closed-groove structures, suggesting that our simulations may be revealing aspects of Ca2+-independent scrambling in mammalian family members.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation results, indicated by 'suggesting' and 'may be revealing'.

claim: The simulations correctly distinguish scrambling-competent structures from non-competent scramblers, but direct comparison of simulation rates with experimental values should be interpreted qualitatively.
source: With regard to predicting absolute rates, our simulations correctly distinguish scrambling-competent structures from non-competent scramblers, but direct comparison of our rates with experimental values (that tend to be 2–3 orders of magnitude slower) should be interpreted qualitatively.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation in quantitative comparison between simulation and experiment.

claim: Single-molecule analysis yielded a scrambling rate of 0.04 events per μs for TMEM16F, whereas the simulations find 3 and 11.3 events per μs for scrambling-competent TMEM16F structures 6QP6* and PDB ID 8B8J, respectively.
source: For example, single-molecule analysis yielded a scrambling rate of 0.04 events per μs for TMEM16F (Watanabe et al., 2018), whereas we find 3 and 11.3 events per μs for our scrambling-competent TMEM16F structures 6QP6* and PDB ID 8B8J, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claim: Malvezzi et al. estimated a scrambling rate of 0.02 events per μs for afTMEM16 using a liposome-based assay, while the simulations find 10.7 events per μs.
source: Malvezzi et al. estimated a similar scrambling rate of 0.02 events per μs for afTMEM16 using a liposome-based assay, while we find 10.7 events per μs (Malvezzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claim: The Martini model increases diffusion dynamics by a factor ~4 due to the lower friction between CG beads and reduced configurational entropy compared to more chemically detailed representations.
source: First, it is well established that the Martini model increases diffusion dynamics by a factor ~4 due to the lower friction between CG beads and reduced configurational entropy compared to more chemically detailed representations (Bruininks et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on the Martini force field.

claim: The energy barrier for a PC headgroup to traverse the DOPC bilayer in the absence of protein is reduced in Martini 3 compared to Martini 2 and AAMD.
source: Second, the energy barrier for a PC headgroup to traverse the DOPC bilayer in the absence of protein is reduced in Martini 3 compared to Martini 2 and AAMD (Bartoš et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing force fields.

claim: It is not trivial to predict how the reduction in energy barrier affects protein-mediated lipid scrambling, but it is likely to increase observed flipping rates compared to the more realistic AAMD.
source: It is not trivial to predict how this reduction affects protein-mediated lipid scrambling, but it is likely to increase observed flipping rates compared to the more realistic AAMD.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the effect of force field differences on simulation results.

claim: The Martini 3 elastic network used to restrain the protein backbone allows a small degree of flexibility during simulations, which may increase scrambling.
source: Third, as shown in Figure 3B, the Martini 3 elastic network used to restrain the protein backbone in our simulations allows a small degree of flexibility during simulations, which may increase scrambling.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the effect of the elastic network on simulation results and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The groove of the open nhTMEM16 structure 4WIS enlarges by ~3 Å during Martini 3 simulations compared to the starting experimental structure and Martini 2 simulations, and this dilation correlates with greater scrambling.
source: For instance, the groove of the open nhTMEM16 structure 4WIS enlarges by ~3 Å during our Martini 3 simulations compared to the starting experimental structure and our Martini 2 simulations, and this dilation correlates with greater scrambling (Appendix 1—figure 8A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: CHARMM36 AAMD trajectories of nhTMEM16 show some degree of dilation, but they generally stay closer to the experimental structure than Martini 3 simulations.
source: We also analyzed previously published CHARMM36 AAMD trajectories starting from the same structure (Bethel and Grabe, 2016) and observed that while these simulations do show some degree of dilation, as we observe with Martini 3, they generally stay closer to the experimental structure (Appendix 1—figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of previously published AAMD data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: Similar subtle movements in the TM4 helix were observed for open Ca2+-bound structures of afTMEM16, TMEM16K, TMEM16F, and TMEM16A that appear to enlarge the TM4/TM6 outer vestibule.
source: In addition to the open nhTMEM16 structure, we observed similar subtle movements in the TM4 helix for open Ca2+-bound structures of afTMEM16, TMEM16K, TMEM16F, and TMEM16A that appear to enlarge the TM4/TM6 outer vestibule (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: AAMD simulations have reported that spontaneous dilation of the groove/pore can confer either scramblase activity for WT and mutant TMEM16F or ion channel activity for TMEM16A structures.
source: Others have reported that AAMD simulations sample spontaneous dilation of the groove/pore to confer either scramblase activity for WT (Le et al., 2019b; Khelashvili et al., 2022) and mutant (Jia et al., 2022) TMEM16F or ion channel activity for TMEM16A structures (Le et al., 2019a; Yu et al., 2019; Tembo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to computational studies.

claim: Movements away from the experimentally solved structures may be due to the inaccuracy of atomistic and CG force fields or differences in the model and experimental membrane/detergent environments.
source: These movements away from the experimentally solved structures may be due to the inaccuracy of our atomistic and CG force fields or differences in the model and experimental membrane/detergent environments, but more work is needed to assess whether these dilations reflect physiologically relevant conformational states.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the causes of observed structural changes in simulations.

claim: CG simulations of closed-groove structures lack dilations because the backbones of TM4 and TM6 are in close enough proximity (<10 Å) to be connected by the elastic network that the Martini model requires to maintain proper secondary and tertiary structure.
source: CG simulations of closed-groove structures lack such dilations, because the backbones of TM4 and TM6 are in close enough proximity (<10 Å) to be connected by the elastic network that the Martini model requires to maintain proper secondary and tertiary structure (e.g., PDB ID 6QM4, see Appendix 1—figure 8C, D).
evidence: This claim is an explanation for the observed behavior in simulations and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The recent GōMartini 3 model replaces the harmonic bonds of the elastic network with Lennard–Jones potentials that vanish as residues separate, potentially making this an excellent model for sampling groove opening and closing.
source: The recent GōMartini 3 model replaces the harmonic bonds of the elastic network with Lennard–Jones potentials that vanish as residues separate, potentially making this an excellent model for sampling groove opening and closing (Souza et al., 2024; Appendix 1—figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the potential of a new force field model and is supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: The low number of recorded scrambling events for TMEM16A (11 for the highest and 1 for the lowest) may be consistent with the lack of experimentally measured scramblase activity.
source: Finally, we end by discussing the observed in- and out-of-the-groove scrambling for the putative ion-conducting states of TMEM16A. The low number of recorded events (11 for the highest and 1 for the lowest) may be consistent with the lack of experimentally measured scramblase activity (Han et al., 2019; Gyobu et al., 2017), for the reasons discussed in the last paragraph.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of simulation results in light of experimental data.

claim: An energy barrier for lipid movement through the TMEM16A groove was computed to be 5.5-fold higher than the scramblase barriers.
source: Consistent with our low computational rate, we also computed an energy barrier for lipid movement through the TMEM16A groove 5.5-fold higher than the scramblase barriers (Appendix 1—figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: In simulations of three predicted ion-conductive states of TMEM16A (7ZK3*6,8,10) lipid headgroups insert into the lower and upper vestibule of the pore.
source: In simulations of our three predicted ion-conductive states of TMEM16A (7ZK3*6,8,10) lipid headgroups insert into the lower and upper vestibule of the pore.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claim: Compared to the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB ID 7ZK3), the outer vestibule of the conductive states of TMEM16A is notably more dilated.
source: Compared to the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB ID 7ZK3), the outer vestibule of these conductive states is notably more dilated.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison from simulation data.

claim: Four Cl− permeation events by TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) were observed through the partially lipid-lined groove.
source: We observe four Cl− permeation events by 7ZK3*8 through the partially lipid-lined groove.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claim: The simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen at times featured a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members.
source: Surprisingly, our simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen did at times feature a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members (Jia and Chen, 2021; Figure 1D, Figure 3—video 1); however, we did not observe any ion permeation events from this configuration, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure and video.

claim: No ion permeation events were observed from the fully lipid-lined groove configuration of TMEM16A, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
source: Surprisingly, our simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen did at times feature a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members (Jia and Chen, 2021; Figure 1D, Figure 3—video 1); however, we did not observe any ion permeation events from this configuration, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
